history.heading: Anatolia's ancient civilisations
paragraphs: Anatolia, the Asian part of Türkiye, is one of the cradles of civilisation. Göbekli Tepe, built around 9500 BCE, is the oldest known monumental temple complex, and Çatalhöyük is one of the earliest towns. The Hittite Empire flourished in the 2nd millennium BCE, and Troy, Lydia (where coins were invented) and Greek cities such as Ephesus were located there.

Anatolia was later part of the Persian, Hellenistic and Roman empires. In 330 CE Constantine made Byzantium, renamed Constantinople, capital of the Roman Empire, which continued as the Byzantine Empire for over a thousand years.

history.heading: Seljuks and Ottomans
paragraphs: Turkic Seljuks defeated the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 and settled Anatolia. Around 1299 Osman I founded the Ottoman state, which captured Constantinople in 1453 under Mehmed II, making it Istanbul.

Under Suleiman the Magnificent in the 16th century, the Ottoman Empire stretched across southeastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa. It gradually declined from the 17th century and entered the First World War on Germany's side. During the war, the Ottoman government carried out the deportation and mass killing of Armenians, recognised as genocide by many countries, though Türkiye rejects the term.

history.heading: The Republic
paragraphs: After the war, Mustafa Kemal (Atatürk) led the War of Independence against occupying powers and founded the Republic of Turkey on 29 October 1923, with Ankara as capital. He introduced sweeping secular reforms: abolishing the caliphate, adopting the Latin alphabet, granting women the vote and Western-style laws.

Turkey joined NATO in 1952. Military coups occurred in 1960, 1971 and 1980. A conflict with the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) from 1984 killed tens of thousands; in 2025 the PKK announced it would disband. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has led the country since 2003, first as prime minister and then as president. A coup attempt in 2016 failed. Devastating earthquakes in February 2023 killed over 50,000 people. The country officially changed its English name to Türkiye in 2022.

culture.heading: Crossroads of East and West
paragraphs: Turkish is the official language, and Kurdish is widely spoken by a large minority. Most people are Muslim, mainly Sunni, with an Alevi minority. Istanbul, spanning Europe and Asia, is home to the Hagia Sophia, the Blue Mosque and Topkapı Palace.

Writer Orhan Pamuk won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2006. Turkish television dramas are popular across the Middle East, Latin America and the Balkans. The whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi order and Turkish coffee are recognised by UNESCO.

culture.heading: Food and traditions
paragraphs: Turkish cuisine includes kebabs, meze, baklava, Turkish delight, börek and simit, with tea drunk throughout the day. Hammams (Turkish baths) and bazaars such as Istanbul's Grand Bazaar are traditions. Football is the most popular sport, along with oil wrestling and volleyball.

politics.heading: Presidential system
paragraphs: Since a 2017 referendum, Türkiye has a strong presidential system. Erdoğan's Justice and Development Party (AKP) has governed since 2002. The main opposition is the secular Republican People's Party (CHP). In 2025 Istanbul's mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, a leading opposition figure, was arrested, triggering mass protests. Critics accuse the government of eroding democracy and press freedom.

Türkiye is a NATO member and an EU candidate, though accession talks have stalled. It plays an active role in Syria, Ukraine, the Caucasus and the Middle East, and hosts the world's largest refugee population, mainly Syrians.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Türkiye has one of the largest economies in Europe and the Middle East. It is a manufacturing hub for cars, textiles, appliances, steel and defence equipment, including drones. Tourism is a major sector, with Istanbul and the Mediterranean coast among the most visited places in the world. Agriculture produces hazelnuts, dried apricots and figs.

Unconventional monetary policies led to very high inflation and a sharp fall of the Turkish lira, peaking at over 80 percent inflation in 2022. Since 2023 the central bank has raised interest rates to bring inflation down.
